chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
question_text: Give examples of "photosensitive substances". Why are they called so?

verification.note: From FAST TRACK IPE for Sr. Students, physics section, Ch.12 (printed p.42); the book prints no exam-year citations for this chapter. The 1+1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. For this Paper-II bank the two-book union check and the past-paper back-test are STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is first-year physics only, and the paper corpus holds only Paper-I papers. Hand-checked physically: the alkali metals sodium, potassium, lithium and caesium have work functions near 2 eV (caesium 2.14 eV), and visible-light photons carry roughly 1.6 to 3.1 eV, so visible light can emit photoelectrons from them. The book's example list also names calcium, zinc, cadmium and magnesium, whose work functions are higher (calcium 3.20 eV against 3.10 eV for a 400 nm photon, and zinc, cadmium and magnesium higher still), so those four need ultraviolet light. The example list is reproduced as the book prints it, but the book's blanket reason — that visible light is enough for all of them — is NOT reproduced: step s2 states the low work function as the reason and names the visible/ultraviolet split, so no line on this card claims visible light works for calcium, zinc, cadmium or magnesium. A lecturer's pen tick marks this question in the source scan as one to expect.

steps.margin_note: First mark. Two or three named metals are enough; the alkali metals are the safest picks.
steps.why: The examiner wants named substances, and the alkali metals head every textbook list because their work functions are the lowest.
common_mistakes: Naming compounds or non-metals. The standard examples are metals.
Giving one example when the question asks for examples. Write at least two.

recall.must_convey: At least two named photosensitive metals, such as sodium, potassium, lithium or caesium.

steps.memory_tip: Start with the alkali metals in order: lithium, sodium, potassium, caesium.

lines.text: Low work function: visible or UV light works

steps.margin_note: Second mark. The reason is the low work function; connect it to light emitting photoelectrons.
steps.why: A visible photon carries about 1.6 to 3.1 eV. Sodium, potassium, lithium and caesium have work functions near 2 eV, so visible light is already enough for them. Calcium (3.2 eV), magnesium, cadmium and zinc are higher, so they need ultraviolet light instead. All eight are still photosensitive because their work functions are low enough for light to remove an electron, unlike platinum at 5.65 eV.
common_mistakes: Saying they are sensitive because they are metals. All the examples are metals; the low work function is the reason.
Writing high work function. The work function must be LOW for light of a suitable frequency to remove an electron.
Saying visible light works for every metal in the list. Calcium, zinc, cadmium and magnesium need ultraviolet light.

recall.must_convey: That these substances have a low work function, so light of a suitable frequency makes them emit photoelectrons.
accept: light makes them give out electrons

steps.memory_tip: Photo plus sensitive: light emits electrons from them, because the work function is low.

insider_note: Examples earn one mark and the reason the other — and the reason must contain the words low work function.
